title: Decentralized Clinical Trials Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2032
executive_summary:
Published estimates of the decentralized clinical trials market agree with each other to an unusual degree, and that is the first thing a reader should be suspicious of. Four independent houses put the 2024 base year between $8.19 billion and $8.8 billion -- a spread of only 1.07x -- and published compound growth rates between 13.0% and 14.8%, a spread of 1.14x. In a literature where eleven-fold disagreements are routine, convergence this tight usually means the houses are deriving the figure the same way from the same upstream denominator, not measuring independently.

The interesting question is therefore not how big the market is but what the agreed number can possibly be counting. ClinicalTrials.gov answers that. Of 607,160 studies in the register on 16 October 2026, exactly 37 text-match the phrase "decentralized clinical trial" -- six thousandths of one percent. There is no population of self-identified decentralized trials large enough to carry a $10 billion market.

What there is, is a population of ordinary industry trials buying decentralized components. 11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, a run-rate of 5,751 a year. Divide the published 2026 market by that and you get $1.77 million of decentralization spend per industry trial -- roughly 2% to 9% of a late-phase budget, which is plausible, but only if essentially every industry trial now carries some decentralized element.

That is also the regulator's position. The FDA issued its final guidance in September 2024 under the title Conducting Clinical Trials With Decentralized Elements, retitling the 2023 draft, which had been Decentralized Clinical Trials for Drugs, Biological Products, and Devices. Commentators read the change as the agency abandoning the attempt to classify whole trials as decentralized or hybrid in favour of regulating individual elements. The commercial confirmation is Science 37, the only listed pure-play: it went public by SPAC merger in 2021 above a $1 billion valuation, booked $70.1 million of revenue in 2022, and sold to eMed in 2024 for about $38 million -- a third of one percent of the market it was named after.
market_context:
Decentralization is not a technology. It is a change in where the trial happens, and it is assembled from components that already had their own markets: telehealth consultations, electronic consent, electronic patient-reported outcome instruments, home nursing visits, direct-to-patient drug shipment, wearable sensors and remote source data verification. A sponsor does not buy a decentralized trial. It buys some of those components and runs them alongside sites.

That structure explains why the market is simultaneously easy to size and impossible to locate. Every large CRO and every eClinical platform vendor sells decentralized components, and none of them reports the revenue separately. Medidata sits inside Dassault Systemes with no standalone disclosure. Veeva reports product families rather than modalities: its 10-K for the year ended 31 January 2026 states that R&D and Quality Solutions was approximately 55% of total revenues of $3,195.3 million, which implies roughly $1.76 billion -- but that is the whole R&D platform, and the 55% is a percentage we have multiplied out ourselves rather than a reported figure. Oracle Health Sciences is consolidated inside Oracle. IQVIA's decentralized capability is spread across its R&D Solutions segment.

The one company that organised itself entirely around the narrow definition demonstrated what that definition is worth. Science 37's $70.1 million of 2022 revenue was 0.69% of the market as published for 2026, and the $38 million eMed paid for the whole company in 2024 was 0.37% of it. A market where the pure-play is a rounding error is a market defined by a feature, not by an industry.
forecast_analysis:
The curve shown here is modelled at a constant rate between two published endpoints. P&S Intelligence, in its April 2026 edition, publishes $9.1 billion for 2025, $10.2 billion for 2026 and $21.4 billion for 2032 with a stated 13.0% CAGR over 2026-2032. Those endpoints imply 13.15% compound, which reconciles with the stated rate. The intermediate years are interpolation, not separately sourced observations.

This series was chosen because it publishes an explicit 2026 value and an explicit 2032 value on one scope, and because its segmentation makes the broad reading of the market explicit: alongside hybrid designs at about 60% and fully decentralized designs in the minority, it carries a category called site-centric with digital enablement. A trial that is site-centric with digital enablement is a conventional trial that bought a decentralized component. Counting it is exactly the scope decision the grounding arithmetic shows must be in force, and P&S is the only house that says so in its own structure.

The forecast endpoints across the set look more divergent than they are. BCC Research reaches $18.8 billion by 2030, Business Research Insights $24.97 billion by 2032 and Global Market Insights $29.7 billion by 2034. Rebased to 2032 at each house's own rate they sit between roughly $21 billion and $25 billion. The real uncertainty is not the rate but whether the category survives as a separate line item at all, given that the regulator has stopped treating it as one.

market_overview.summary: On the scope used by the most recent series that publishes both a 2026 and a 2032 value, the decentralized clinical trials market is $10.2 billion in 2026, projected to $21.4 billion by 2032 at a 13.0% CAGR. Published 2024 base-year estimates span only $8.19 billion to $8.8 billion, a 1.07x spread, and published growth rates only 13.0% to 14.8%. That agreement is unusual and should be read as a shared derivation method rather than as corroboration. Against ClinicalTrials.gov, only 37 of 607,160 registered studies describe themselves as decentralized trials, so the published figures can only be measuring decentralized elements bought by ordinary industry trials -- which is also how the FDA chose to regulate them from September 2024.
key_trends: Published 2024 base-year estimates span just 1.07x ($8.19 billion to $8.8 billion) and CAGRs just 1.14x (13.0% to 14.8%), the tightest agreement in this corpus
Only 37 of the 607,160 studies in ClinicalTrials.gov text-match "decentralized clinical trial" as of 16 October 2026, which is 0.006% of the register
11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, implying $1.77 million of decentralization spend per industry trial at the published 2026 market size
The FDA's September 2024 final guidance is titled Conducting Clinical Trials With Decentralized Elements, retitled from a 2023 draft that had named decentralized trials as a trial class
Science 37, the only listed pure-play, sold to eMed for about $38 million in 2024 after a 2021 SPAC merger above a $1 billion valuation and $70.1 million of 2022 revenue
P&S Intelligence's own segmentation carries site-centric with digital enablement as a category, confirming that conventional trials with decentralized components are inside the count
market_overview.adoption_level: Component-level adoption is widespread in industry trials; fully remote designs remain a minority

drivers: A regulatory framework that now explicitly accommodates decentralized elements: the FDA's final guidance of September 2024 covers telehealth visits, in-home visits by remote trial personnel and visits with local healthcare providers
A very large base of ordinary trials into which components can be sold: 11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, a run-rate of 5,751 a year
Recruitment and retention economics, which decentralized elements improve by removing travel from the participant's burden rather than by changing the science
Rare disease and oncology programmes where the eligible population is geographically dispersed and site-based recruitment is the binding constraint
Established eClinical platform vendors able to add decentralized modules to installed bases they already own, which lowers the cost of adoption for sponsors
restraints: The FDA's retitling of its own guidance removed the regulatory basis for treating decentralized trials as a distinct class, which undermines the category as a separately purchasable line item
Only 37 studies in a 607,160-study register describe themselves as decentralized, so there is no self-identifying buyer population to sell to
The only listed pure-play, Science 37, reached $70.1 million of revenue and sold for about $38 million in 2024, which is the market's own verdict on standalone decentralized businesses
Investigational product complexity limits what can leave the site: the FDA's guidance advises weighing product safety and complexity, with in-person oversight for high-risk or first-in-human products
Published market sizes that converge too neatly on a figure none of the houses can decompose make this category an unreliable basis for capital planning
opportunities: Selling decentralized components into the large majority of trials that remain site-centric, which is where P&S Intelligence locates a named segment rather than a new market
Post-approval and real-world late-phase studies, which P&S identifies as the fastest-growing phase category and where home-based data collection is the default rather than an innovation
Small and medium sponsors, identified as the fastest-growing organisation size, who have no site network to protect and therefore no internal resistance to decentralization
Regulatory operations services: sponsors now need to document how each decentralized element was controlled, which creates work that did not exist before September 2024
challenges: No participant discloses decentralized-trial revenue, so share cannot be computed for anyone: Medidata sits inside Dassault Systemes, Oracle Health Sciences inside Oracle, and Veeva reports product families rather than modalities
Component-level adoption inside conventional trials is invisible to every public register, so adoption cannot be measured, only asserted
Local healthcare provider involvement shifts responsibility to clinicians who are not trial-trained, which is a quality risk the FDA guidance addresses but does not remove
The convergence of published estimates removes the usual diagnostic signal: when houses disagree you can locate the scope decision, and when they agree without publishing methods you cannot

research_methodology.data_validation: Market size is taken from published third-party estimates and attributed to each house by name; no methodology behind those estimates was inspected, and they are presented as published estimates rather than as verified measurements. Three plausibility tests were run against countable public records. First, of 607,160 studies in ClinicalTrials.gov on 16 October 2026 only 37 text-match "decentralized clinical trial" -- 0.006% -- which rules out any reading in which the market consists of self-identified decentralized trials. Second, 11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, a run-rate of 5,751 a year; dividing the published 2026 market of $10.2 billion by that gives $1,773,605 per trial, roughly 2% to 9% of a late-phase budget, which is plausible only if essentially every industry trial carries some decentralized element -- the same reading the FDA adopted when it retitled its guidance in September 2024. Third, Science 37, the only listed pure-play, booked $70.1 million in 2022 (0.69% of the published 2026 market) and sold for about $38 million in 2024 (0.37%), which rules out a reading in which the market consists of standalone decentralized-trial businesses. None of these tests establishes the correct market size and none is offered as an estimate. The 2032 endpoint and intermediate years are interpolation between P&S Intelligence's published 2026 and 2032 values at the implied constant rate, not separately published observations.

faqs.question: How big is the decentralized clinical trials market?
faqs.answer: $10.2 billion in 2026 rising to $21.4 billion by 2032 at 13.0%, on the scope published by P&S Intelligence in April 2026. Published 2024 base-year estimates from four houses run only $8.19 billion to $8.8 billion, a 1.07x spread, which is unusually tight. Treat that agreement as a shared derivation method rather than as independent corroboration, because none of the houses publishes the method.

faqs.question: Why do so few registered trials describe themselves as decentralized?
faqs.answer: Because almost none of them are, in the strict sense. On 16 October 2026 exactly 37 of the 607,160 studies in ClinicalTrials.gov text-matched the phrase "decentralized clinical trial". A $10 billion market cannot rest on 37 studies, so the published figures must be counting decentralized components bought by ordinary trials. The FDA reached the same conclusion: its September 2024 final guidance is titled Conducting Clinical Trials With Decentralized Elements, having dropped the 2023 draft's framing of decentralized trials as a trial class.

faqs.question: How can you check whether a decentralized trials market size is plausible?
faqs.answer: Divide it by the number of trials that could buy decentralized components. 11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, a run-rate of 5,751 a year. $10.2 billion over that is $1,773,605 per trial, or about 2% to 9% of a typical late-phase budget. That passes -- but only on the assumption that nearly every industry trial now buys something decentralized. If you believe only a minority do, the implied per-trial spend becomes impossible.

faqs.question: What happened to the pure-play decentralized trial companies?
faqs.answer: Science 37, the only listed one, went public by SPAC merger in 2021 at a valuation above $1 billion, reached $70.1 million of revenue in 2022 against a $100 million forecast, and was acquired by eMed in 2024 for $5.75 per share, about $38 million. Its best reported year was 0.69% of the market as published for 2026, and the whole company sold for 0.37% of it. That is the clearest evidence that decentralization is a feature sold by incumbents, not an industry.

faqs.question: Who leads the decentralized clinical trials market?
faqs.answer: IQVIA, Medidata, Veeva Systems and Oracle Health Sciences are the recognised participants, and not one of them discloses decentralized-trial revenue. Medidata sits inside Dassault Systemes. Oracle Health Sciences sits inside Oracle. Veeva reports product families: its 10-K puts R&D and Quality Solutions at approximately 55% of $3,195.3 million for the year ended 31 January 2026, which is the whole R&D platform. No share percentage exists for anyone, so treat any you are shown as unsourced.

faqs.question: Why does this report show no regional breakdown?
faqs.answer: Because no named source publishes a defensible dollar split for this scope. P&S Intelligence states North America at about 40% and Asia-Pacific growing fastest at 13.9%, but publishes no regional values and no method. We have a global trial register and no regional revenue data, which is enough to test a global figure for plausibility and not enough to apportion one, so the section is omitted.

key_highlights: Published 2024 base-year estimates span only 1.07x ($8.19 billion to $8.8 billion) and CAGRs only 1.14x (13.0% to 14.8%) -- read the agreement as a shared method, not as corroboration
Only 37 of 607,160 studies in ClinicalTrials.gov text-match "decentralized clinical trial" as of 16 October 2026, which is 0.006% of the register
11,502 industry-sponsored interventional studies began across 2024 and 2025, implying $1,773,605 of decentralization spend per industry trial at the published 2026 size
The FDA's September 2024 final guidance regulates decentralized elements, not decentralized trials, having retitled the 2023 draft that treated them as a trial class
Science 37, the only listed pure-play, booked $70.1 million in 2022 and sold to eMed for about $38 million in 2024 -- 0.37% of the market it was named after
P&S Intelligence's own segmentation includes site-centric trials with digital enablement, confirming conventional trials are inside the count
No participant discloses decentralized-trial revenue, so no share figure for this market is verifiable
reader_takeaways: Before accepting a decentralized trials market size, ask whether it counts trials or components -- only the component reading survives the 37-studies-in-607,160 test

Use ClinicalTrials.gov as your own sanity check: divide any figure you are given by roughly 5,751 industry-sponsored interventional trials a year and ask whether that per-trial spend is credible for your therapeutic area
Read the FDA's September 2024 retitling as a commercial signal, not just a regulatory one: a category the regulator declines to define as a class is hard to sell as a line item
Do not plan on a standalone decentralized business: the only pure-play reached $70.1 million of revenue and sold for about $38 million
Treat any vendor share percentage for this market as unsourced, because every significant participant reports decentralization inside a larger segment or inside a parent company

seo.meta_description: DCT estimates agree within 1.07x, yet only 37 of 607,160 ClinicalTrials.gov studies call themselves decentralized. What the published figures count.
